seo.h1: Skilled Migration to Australia: Choose Your Visa Pathway

hero.h1: Skilled Migration to Australia: Choose Your Visa Pathway
intro: Australia invites skilled people to live and work here permanently. There are three main points-tested visas, and the right one depends on your occupation, your points and where you are willing to live. Our registered migration agents in Melbourne and Adelaide explain each option in plain English and tell you what to do next.

sections.name: Who this is for
sections.h2: Is skilled migration right for you?

blocks.x: Skilled migration suits you if you have a qualification and work experience in an occupation Australia needs. Most people fall into one of three groups. The requirements are set out in [how skilled migration works](/skilled-migration).

items.x: **Graduates studying or working in Australia.** You may hold a Temporary Graduate visa (subclass 485). You can use Australian study points, regional study points and a state nomination. See [Temporary Graduate visa (485)](/migrate-to-australia/temporary-graduate-visa-subclass-485).
**Skilled professionals overseas.** You have a degree and several years in fields such as health, engineering, IT, teaching or accounting. You will need a skills assessment before you can be invited.
**Tradespeople.** Electricians, chefs, mechanics, carpenters and plumbers need a trade skills assessment from the assessing authority for your occupation.

blocks.x: Not sure which group you are in? [Book a consultation](/book-an-appointment) and we will check.
Select a visa name to open its guide.

blocks.x: Ask yourself these questions in this order.

items.x: **Is your occupation on the Skilled Occupation List?** Use our [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder). If it is not, 189 is not available.

**How many points do you have?** Use the [PR Points Calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator). A high score may support 189. A lower score may still work with the extra points from a state nomination.

**Will a state nominate your occupation?** States publish their own lists and requirements. For [Victoria, try the Victorian Points Test](/migrate-to-australia/victorian-points-test). For [South Australia, see South Australia state nomination](/south-australia-state-nomination).
**Are you willing to live in a regional area?** If yes, 491 may give you more options. Check a [suburb with the Postcode Checker](/postcode-checker).
**Do you need a faster, safer route?** A registered agent can compare your realistic pathways. No one can promise an invitation.

faqs.q: What is the easiest skilled visa to get?
faqs.a: No skilled visa is easy, and none is guaranteed. The best route depends on your occupation, points, age and willingness to live outside a capital city. A registered agent can compare them for you.

faqs.q: What is the minimum points score for skilled migration?
faqs.a: You need at least 65 points to submit an Expression of Interest for 189, 190 or 491. (Source: Department of Home Affairs, checked 12 November 2026.) In practice, invitations often go to higher scores.

faqs.q: Do I need work experience to apply?
faqs.a: Not always. Points for skilled employment are optional. Some graduates reach a competitive score through English, Australian study, regional study and other points. You still need a positive skills assessment.

faqs.q: Is the 485 visa a permanent visa?
faqs.a: No. It is a temporary post-study work visa. It can help you gain experience and a skills assessment for a points-tested visa.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 190 and 491?
faqs.a: Both need nomination. The 190 is permanent and gives 5 points. The 491 is provisional, gives 15 points and requires you to live and work in a designated regional area.

faqs.q: Can I include my partner and children?
faqs.a: Usually yes, as secondary applicants. Your partner may also add points if they meet the criteria.

faqs.q: How long does it take?
faqs.a: It depends on the assessment, invitation round and visa processing.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee an invitation or visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs or a state government decides. We tell you honestly what is realistic.

cta.text: Bring your qualifications, work history and English test result. We will help you choose your pathway and next step.

seo.title: How Skilled Migration Works in Australia | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: How Australian skilled migration works: skills assessment, points, SkillSelect and invitations. Plan your PR with a Melbourne migration agent.
seo.h1: How Skilled Migration to Australia Works

hero.h1: How Skilled Migration to Australia Works
intro: Skilled migration is a points-based system. You prove your skills, claim your points, express interest and wait for an invitation. This guide explains each stage so you know what to expect before you spend money. Want to compare the visas themselves? Go to our [skilled visa options](/migrate-to-australia).

sections.name: The system in one minute
sections.h2: The skilled migration system in four steps

items.x: **Skills assessment.** An assessing authority confirms your qualification and experience match your occupation.
**Points.** You claim points for age, English, qualifications, experience and other factors.
**Expression of Interest (EOI).** You lodge an EOI in SkillSelect. This is not a visa application.
**Invitation and visa application.** The Department of Home Affairs, or a state or territory, invites the highest-ranking people. Only then can you lodge a visa application.

blocks.x: The three points-tested visas are the Skilled Independent (189), Skilled Nominated (190) and Skilled Work Regional (491). They are also called General Skilled Migration (GSM).

sections.name: The five requirements
sections.h2: What you must have before you can be invited

items.x: **Age under 45** when you are invited.
**Competent English** at minimum. IELTS 6 in each band, or an equivalent test score, is the usual benchmark.
**A suitable skills assessment** for an occupation on the relevant list.
**At least 65 points.** (Source: Department of Home Affairs, checked 12 November 2026.)
**An invitation to apply.** You cannot lodge a 189, 190 or 491 without one.

blocks.x: You and any family on your application must also meet health and character requirements.

sections.name: Points test overview
sections.h2: The points test at a glance

blocks.x: Points are claimed in your EOI and checked at the time of invitation. Here is the overview. For the full table and a worked example, [read how points are calculated](/skilled-migration/how-points-are-calculated).

head: Factor
Points range (summary)
rows: Up to 20 points, overseas and Australian combined
Australian study, regional study, Professional Year, NAATI, specialist education

blocks.x: Figures as per Department of Home Affairs points table.
**Do I need years of work experience?** No. Skilled employment adds points but is not compulsory for the points test. Many graduates score through English, Australian study and regional study.

Your nominated occupation must be on the Skilled Occupation List that applies to your visa. Each occupation has an assessing authority, for example Engineers Australia, ACS, VETASSESS or Trades Recognition Australia. Assessment can take weeks or months, so start early.
State and territory governments also publish their own lists for 190 and 491 nominations. These can differ from the national list.
Use the [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder) to find your occupation code and assessing authority.

sections.name: SkillSelect and invitations
sections.h2: What happens after you lodge an Expression of Interest

blocks.x: SkillSelect ranks EOIs by points, then by the date you reached that score. Invitation rounds depend on the number of places for each occupation. A high score does not guarantee an invitation, and a score of exactly 65 is rarely enough in a competitive occupation.

State nomination works separately. Each state invites people from SkillSelect to apply for nomination, using its own criteria. For [Victoria, see the Victorian Points Test](/migrate-to-australia/victorian-points-test). For [South Australia, see state nomination](/south-australia-state-nomination).
Your EOI stays valid for a limited period.

items.x: Claiming points you cannot prove with documents.
Claiming English points from a test that has expired.
Choosing an occupation by interest, not by evidence of your actual duties.
Assuming a 485 visa leads straight to PR.
Missing the age cut-off by a few days.
Ignoring a partner's skills or English, which can change your score.
Compare the visas in [skilled visa options](/migrate-to-australia).
Check your occupation with the [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder).
Estimate your points with the [PR Points Calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator).
Read the [step-by-step migration process](/migrate-to-australia/migration) to plan documents and costs.

blocks.x: A registered agent can review your qualifications, points and evidence before you spend money on tests or assessments. We cannot promise an invitation or a visa.

faqs.q: What is General Skilled Migration?
faqs.a: It is the group of points-tested visas for skilled workers: subclasses 189, 190 and 491.

faqs.q: Is an EOI the same as a visa application?
faqs.a: No. An EOI tells the Department you are interested. You can apply for the visa only after an invitation.

faqs.q: How many points do I need?
faqs.a: At least 65 to submit an EOI. Invitations often need more, depending on the occupation and round.

faqs.q: Do I need a job offer?
faqs.a: Not for 189, 190 or 491. These visas are not employer-sponsored. For [employer routes, see employer-sponsored visas](/employer-sponsored).

faqs.q: Can I improve my score?
faqs.a: Often yes. Higher English, a Professional Year, regional study, NAATI credentials and a partner's skills can add points. See [how points are calculated](/skilled-migration/how-points-are-calculated).

faqs.q: How long does the whole process take?
faqs.a: It varies widely. Skills assessment, invitation and visa processing each take time. See the [step-by-step guide](/migrate-to-australia/migration).

faqs.q: Can you guarantee an invitation?
faqs.a: No. We do not guarantee outcomes.

seo.h1: The Migration Process to Australia: Step by Step

hero.h1: The Migration Process to Australia: Step by Step
intro: Moving to Australia as a skilled worker takes several stages, and each one has its own rules. This guide walks you through them in order, from checking your occupation to arriving on your visa. It shows what you do, what the Department does and where people usually lose time.

blocks.x: This is the general skilled route. Employer-sponsored and partner visas follow different steps. See [employer-sponsored visas](/employer-sponsored) and [family visas](/family-visa).

items.x: **Choose your pathway.** Decide between 189, 190 and 491. Your occupation, points and willingness to live regionally drive this choice. Read the [visa comparison](/migrate-to-australia).

**Check your occupation.** Search the [Occupation Finder](/occupation-finder). Note the code and the assessing authority. If your occupation is not on any list, ask us about other options before you spend money.
**Take an English test.** Competent English is the minimum. Higher scores earn points. Book early, because results are valid for a limited time.

**Get a skills assessment.** Apply to the assessing authority for your occupation. You will usually provide identity documents, qualifications, transcripts, employment references and payslips or tax records. Processing times vary by authority.

**Calculate your points and lodge an EOI.** Use the [PR Points Calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator) and read [how points are calculated](/skilled-migration/how-points-are-calculated). Lodge your Expression of Interest in SkillSelect. You need at least 65 points.

**Get nominated (190 and 491 only).** Apply to a state or territory under its own rules. See the [Victorian Points Test](/migrate-to-australia/victorian-points-test) and [South Australia state nomination](/south-australia-state-nomination).
**Receive an invitation and lodge your visa.** You have a limited time after an invitation to lodge. Pay the visa application charge and upload your documents.

**Complete health and police checks.** You may need health examinations and police certificates for every country where you lived for a set period. See our [AFP police check](/afp-national-police-check) page. After the decision, check your visa conditions and the date by which you must first enter Australia.

Degree certificates and academic transcripts
Employment references, contracts, payslips and tax records
English test results

Police certificates and health examination results (when requested)

blocks.x: Gather these before you need them. Gaps in employment evidence are a common cause of delay.
Time and cost depend on the pathway, so we do not give a single number.

sections.name: Mistakes that cause delay or refusal
sections.h2: Mistakes that cause delay or refusal

items.x: Starting with the visa and leaving the skills assessment until late.
Claiming points you cannot prove.
Letting an English test expire.
Using an occupation that does not match your real duties.
Not disclosing earlier visa refusals or character issues.
Missing the deadline after an invitation.

blocks.x: If a visa is refused, review rights are time-limited. See [visa refusal](/appeals/visa-refusal).

Once you hold an invitation and a visa, see the guide for your visa: [189](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-independent-visa-subclass-189), [190](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-nominated-visa-subclass-190) or [491](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-work-regional-provisional-visa-subclass-491). Regional visa holders can later apply for the [191](/migrate-to-australia/permanent-residence-skilled-regional-visa-subclass-191).

You can lodge applications yourself. People often ask for help when their occupation is borderline, they have a past refusal, their work history has gaps, or they want to compare 189, 190 and 491. Our registered agents explain the options and the risks. You decide whether to engage us.

[Skilled Nominated Visa (Subclass 190)](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-nominated-visa-subclass-190)
[Skilled Work Regional Provisional Visa (Subclass 491)](/migrate-to-australia/skilled-work-regional-provisional-visa-subclass-491)
[PR points calculator](/migrate-to-australia/pr-point-calculator)
[Occupation finder](/occupation-finder)
[Skills assessment](/skill-assessment)

faqs.q: How long does the Australian PR process take?
faqs.a: It varies. Add the time for skills assessment, waiting for an invitation, nomination if needed and visa processing.

faqs.q: What is the first step?
faqs.a: Check your occupation and its assessing authority. Then check your points.

faqs.q: Do I need an agent?
faqs.a: No, but a registered agent can help avoid costly mistakes.

faqs.q: Can I apply from inside Australia?
faqs.a: Yes. Many 189, 190 and 491 applicants are in Australia on a student or Temporary Graduate visa. See [485 eligibility](/migrate-to-australia/temporary-graduate-visa-subclass-485).

faqs.q: What if my points are below 65?
faqs.a: You cannot lodge an EOI. You may improve English, gain experience or consider a regional route.

faqs.q: Is a job offer needed?
faqs.a: Not for these visas.

faqs.q: Can my family come with me?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Partners and dependent children can be included.

seo.title: Temporary Graduate Visa In Australia | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Allows international students to live, work, and study in Australia after completing their studies. It’s a popular post-study visa providing valuable work.

intro: Allows international students to live, work, and study in Australia after completing their studies. It’s a popular post-study visa providing valuable work experience and a pathway to permanent residency.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: No set time. Check the Department's guide

blocks.x: The **Temporary Graduate Visa (Subclass 485)** is a temporary visa for international students who have recently graduated from an Australian educational institution. This visa allows you to live, work, and study in Australia temporarily after completing your studies, providing valuable Australian work experience and a potential pathway to permanent residence.
The Subclass 485 offers **three distinct streams** to suit different qualifications and circumstances:

items.x: **Post-Vocational Education Work stream**: For graduates with an associate degree, diploma, or trade qualification that is closely related to an occupation on the Medium and Long-term Strategic Skills List. The stay is up to 18 months.
**Post-Higher Education Work Stream**: For graduates with bachelor's degrees or higher from Australian institutions (2-3 years depending on qualification)
**Second Post-Higher Education Work Stream**: For previous Subclass 485 holders who studied in regional Australia (additional 1-2 years)

blocks.x: **Special provision:** Hong Kong SAR and British National (Overseas) passport holders may stay for 5 years under eligible streams, providing extended opportunities to gain Australian work experience.

sections.name: Eligibility
sections.h2: Do You Have What It Takes?

items.x: Must have recently graduated from an Australian educational institution with eligible qualification
Be in Australia when you apply, hold an eligible visa, and have held a student visa in the last 6 months
Meet Australian study requirement (at least 2 years study in Australia in CRICOS-registered course)
Apply within 6 months of course completion date

Be 35 or under when you apply. You can be under 50 if you use a masters by research or a doctoral degree to meet the study requirement, or if you hold a Hong Kong or British National (Overseas) passport.

Hold adequate health insurance, such as Overseas Visitor Health Cover. Meet the Temporary Graduate English requirement. For IELTS, that is an overall score of 6.5, with at least 5.5 in each part. This is higher than Competent English.
Meet health and character requirements
For the Post-Vocational Education Work stream: nominate an occupation on the Medium and Long-term Strategic Skills List and include a skills assessment for that occupation
For Second stream: previously held Subclass 485 and studied/lived in regional Australia
Gain Australian work experience to increase points for permanent residence applications
Work unlimited hours for any employer in any occupation across Australia
Bring family members - include spouse/partner and dependent children in application
Study further in Australia without restrictions on course type or duration
Travel freely in and out of Australia during visa validity period
Pathway to permanent residence through skilled migration programs (subclass 189, 190, 491)

No sponsorship required - complete freedom to choose employers and change jobs Extended stay for Hong Kong/BN(O) passport holders, up to 5 years in eligible streams. Regional opportunities, second visa option for regional graduates (additional 1-2 years). Build professional networks and establish career in Australian job market.
Complete your Australian qualification and receive completion letter from institution
Check eligibility. Confirm your qualification, the Australian study requirement, and that you are 35 or under, unless an age exception applies.
Obtain skills assessment (Post-Vocational stream only) from relevant assessing authority for nominated occupation
Complete an English test. For IELTS, you need an overall score of 6.5, with at least 5.5 in each part, or the equivalent result on an accepted test.
Arrange health insurance - obtain Overseas Visitor Health Cover (OVHC) for visa duration Lodge visa application within 6 months of course completion date through ImmiAccount

Complete health examinations with approved panel physicians and provide police certificates Upload all supporting documents - qualification certificates, transcripts, CoE, health insurance, English test results
Receive visa grant notification and commence work/further study in Australia
**Initial Duration.** Temporary

blocks.x: Pathway to Permanent Residence

Subclass 485 visa holders can use Australian work experience gained during this visa to apply for permanent residence through skilled migration programs (Subclass 189, 190, 491). Australian work experience adds significant points to skilled visa applications. Many graduates successfully transition to permanent residence after 1-3 years of skilled employment, improved English scores, and meeting state nomination requirements. This visa is specifically designed as a bridge to permanent residence.

There is no set processing time. Use the Department of Home Affairs [visa processing time guide](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-processing-times/global-visa-processing-times). It shows how long recent applications took. It is a guide only, not a promise for your application.

faqs.q: 1. What is the Temporary Graduate Visa (Subclass 485)?
faqs.a: The Temporary Graduate Visa (Subclass 485) allows eligible international graduates to live, work, and study in Australia after completing a CRICOS-registered course.

faqs.q: 2. How long can I stay in Australia on a 485 visa?
faqs.a: The stay duration depends on your stream and qualification — usually up to 18 months for vocational graduates, 2–3 years for higher education graduates, and up to 5 years for Hong Kong or British National Overseas passport holders.

faqs.q: 3. Can I include family members in my 485 visa?
faqs.a: Yes, you can include your eligible partner and dependent children in your application. They must meet all health and character requirements.

faqs.q: 4. Do I need a job offer to apply for a 485 visa?
faqs.a: No, you don’t need a job offer. This visa allows you to gain valuable post-study work experience in Australia without employer sponsorship.

faqs.q: 5. Can I apply for permanent residency after a 485 visa?
faqs.a: Yes, the 485 visa provides a strong pathway toward Permanent Residency through skilled migration, regional sponsorship, or employer-sponsored visas.

faqs.q: 6. Do I need health insurance for a 485 visa?
faqs.a: Yes, you must maintain adequate health insurance (Overseas Visitor Health Cover) during your entire stay in Australia.

faqs.q: 1. What is the Subclass 189 visa?
faqs.a: The Subclass 189 is a points-tested permanent residency visa for skilled workers not sponsored by an employer, state, or family. It allows you to live, work, and study anywhere in Australia permanently.

faqs.q: 2. How many points do I need for a 189 visa?
faqs.a: You need a minimum of 65 points to submit an Expression of Interest (EOI). However, higher scores (80–90+) are often required in competitive occupations like IT, engineering, and healthcare.

faqs.q: 3. How do I apply for a 189 visa?
faqs.a: The application process involves: Skill assessment English test Submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) on SkillSelect Wait for an invitation Apply within 60 days of the invitation

faqs.q: 4. How are invitations issued under the 189 visa?
faqs.a: Invitations are issued through SkillSelect, ranked by points. The Department of Home Affairs conducts invitation rounds based on occupation ceilings and current demand. Occupations in high demand may receive more invitations.

faqs.q: 5. Can I include my de facto partner or children in the application?
faqs.a: Yes. You can include your spouse, de facto partner, and dependent children. They will be granted the same permanent residency rights as you if the visa is approved.

faqs.q: 6. What is the occupation ceiling and how does it affect me?
faqs.a: The occupation ceiling limits how many invitations are issued for each occupation annually. If your occupation hits its ceiling early, you may not receive an invitation, even with a high points score.

faqs.a: Yes, you can apply for PR through the Subclass 191 visa after meeting 3-year work and income requirements.

faqs.q: Is the 491 visa points-tested?
faqs.a: Yes, it requires you to meet the points test threshold (usually 65 points or more).

faqs.q: Can I include family members in my 491 visa?
faqs.a: Yes, eligible family members can be included in your application.

faqs.q: Can I move to a major city while on a 491 visa?
faqs.a: No, you must live, work, and study only in designated regional areas.

faqs.q: What is an employer sponsored visa?
faqs.a: It is a visa where an Australian business supports your application. The business is approved as a sponsor and nominates your job. You then apply for the visa. Some visas are temporary and some are permanent.

faqs.q: Can I sponsor myself?
faqs.a: No. The sponsor must be a separate, genuine business. If you own the business, special rules apply and the Department looks closely at whether the job is genuine. Speak to an agent before you start.

faqs.q: Who pays for the sponsorship?
faqs.a: The employer pays the sponsorship, nomination and SAF levy costs, and cannot recover them from the worker. The visa application charge can be paid by either side.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the 482 and the 186?
faqs.a: The 482 is a temporary visa, up to four years. The 186 is permanent. Many 482 holders move to a 186 through the Temporary Residence Transition stream. Read the [482 page](/employer-sponsored/sid-visa-482) and the [186 TRT page](/employer-sponsored/ens-186-trt).

faqs.q: Does the employer have to advertise the job first?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Labour market testing applies to some nominations and not others. See the [Position Nomination Process Guide](/employer-sponsored/nomination-process).

faqs.q: Can I change employers on a sponsored visa?
faqs.a: Usually you can, but a new employer must be an approved sponsor and nominate you, and you must stay within the time limits that apply to you. Get advice before you resign.

faqs.q: How long does it take?
faqs.a: It depends on the visa and the Department's workload. The three stages together usually take several months.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee the visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides visa applications. We tell you honestly whether your case looks realistic before you spend money.

cta.text: Tell us whether you are the worker or the employer, and what you need. We reply within one business day.

seo.description: A Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA) is a formal five-year agreement between the Australian Government and a regional, state, or territory.

intro: A Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA) is a formal five-year agreement between the Australian Government and a regional, state, or territory authority that allows employers in specific regions to sponsor overseas workers for positions that can’t be filled locally, using tailored terms and concessions beyond the standard skilled migration program.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: The charge for the visa you use
No set time. Check the Department's guide
Pathway to Permanent Residency through ENS 186

blocks.x: The **DAMA program** provides a flexible and region-specific approach to skilled migration, addressing critical labour shortages and supporting economic growth in regional Australia. Each DAMA operates under a **two-tier framework**:

items.x: A **Head Agreement** between the Commonwealth and a regional representative body (Designated Area Representative – DAR).
**Individual DAMA Labour Agreements** between the Department of Home Affairs and approved local employers endorsed by the DAR.

blocks.x: Through a DAMA, employers can access both **skilled and semi-skilled occupations**, often with **concessions** to requirements like English language, salary level (TSMIT), and age limits. DAMAs support regional communities by filling labour gaps while ensuring Australian workers remain the first priority for recruitment.

Currently, there are **13 active DAMAs** across Australia, covering designated regional zones such as the Northern Territory, Pilbara, Orana, Townsville, the Goldfields, Far North Queensland, and others.

blocks.x: Pathway to Permanent Residency through ENS 186

Employers operating under a Designated Area Migration Agreement (DAMA) can sponsor skilled and semi-skilled overseas workers through multiple visa pathways, with the most significant being the pathway to permanent residency through the Employer Nomination Scheme (ENS) Subclass 186 visa. DAMA labour agreements operate within the ENS 186 visa program framework, allowing regional employers who have obtained individual DAMA labour agreements to nominate overseas workers for direct permanent residency with negotiated concessions to standard skilled migration criteria.

There is no set processing time. Use the Department of Home Affairs [visa processing time guide](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-processing-times/global-visa-processing-times). It shows how long recent applications took. It is a guide only, not a promise for your application.
A DAMA agreement does not have its own visa charge. You pay the charge for the visa in the agreement, usually the subclass 482 or the subclass 494.
The subclass 482 base charge is AUD 4,015. The subclass 494 base charge is AUD 6,140. Additional applicant charges are on those pages.

intro: The Skilled Employer Sponsored Regional (Provisional) visa (subclass 494) allows skilled workers to live, work, and study in designated regional areas of Australia for up to 5 years when sponsored by an approved employer to fill local skill shortages, with a pathway to permanent residence after 3 years.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: No set time. Check the Department's guide

blocks.x: The **Subclass 494 Skilled Employer Sponsored Regional (Provisional) visa** helps **regional Australian employers** fill positions they cannot find suitable Australian workers for by sponsoring skilled migrants. This visa promotes regional development by directing skilled workers to designated regional areas outside metropolitan Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, and other non-regional zones.

It includes the **Employer Sponsored stream**, **Labour Agreement stream**, and **Subsequent Entrant option**. Holders can live and work exclusively in regional Australia for up to 5 years and apply for permanent residence after 3 years (through the **Subclass 191 Permanent Residence (Skilled Regional)** visa). Eligible family members can also join the primary visa holder.

sections.name: Eligibility
sections.h2: Do You Have What It Takes?

items.x: You are nominated by an approved regional employer.
Your occupation is on the relevant skilled occupation list.
You hold a valid skills assessment in your nominated occupation.
You are under 45 years of age (unless exempt).
You meet English language requirements.

intro: The Temporary Activity visa (subclass 408) allows individuals to come to Australia for short-term work or activities related to specific cultural, sporting, entertainment, educational, or government-endorsed events. The visa duration depends on the activity, ranging from a few months to up to 4 years, and usually requires sponsorship or support by an Australian organization.

blocks.x: The **Subclass 408 visa** offers multiple streams for people wishing to visit Australia to undertake **short-term, temporary activities** such as cultural exchange, sports, entertainment, religious work, research, or participation in government-endorsed events. Family members can usually be included, and costs for the main applicant start from **AUD 535**.

intro: Complete guide to Standard Business Sponsorship for Australian employers who want to sponsor overseas workers for temporary and permanent work visas.

blocks.x: Standard Business Sponsorship (SBS)

Standard Business Sponsorship (SBS) is the foundation of employer-sponsored visa programs in Australia. It is the approval that allows businesses to sponsor skilled overseas workers for temporary work visas (such as the 482) and certain pathways to permanent residency (186).
SBS is **not a visa** - it is an approval status for your business that demonstrates to the Department of Home Affairs that you are:

items.x: A legitimate, lawfully operating business in Australia
Capable of meeting sponsorship obligations
Committed to training Australian workers
Able to pay market salary rates
Willing to provide fair working conditions

blocks.x: Once approved, your SBS lasts for **5 years** and allows you to nominate multiple overseas workers during that period.
You need SBS if you want to sponsor workers for:

items.x: **Skill in Demand visa (482):** Temporary skilled workers
**Training visa (407):** Workplace-based training programs
**ENS 186 (some streams):** Permanent residency pathways
**Regional 494:** Regional skilled workers
**Be lawfully operating in Australia** - registered with ASIC or relevant authority
**Have a genuine need** for skilled overseas workers
**Be financially viable** - able to pay the nominated employee
**Have no adverse information** - no history of non-compliance with immigration or workplace laws
**Meet training requirements** - either meet training benchmarks OR pay the SAF levy when nominating
Pay market salary rates (minimum $70,000 for most positions)
Provide terms and conditions no less favorable than Australian workers
Cooperate with inspectors and monitoring activities
Keep accurate records for at least 2 years after sponsorship ends
Not recover costs from the sponsored worker
Notify the Department of certain changes (e.g., worker no longer employed)
Business registration documents (ABN, ASIC registration)
Evidence of lawful operation (tax returns, BAS statements)
Organizational structure chart
Evidence of training commitment
Statutory declaration of compliance

blocks.x: Typically **3-5 business days** from lodgement to decision.
**$420** application fee
As a sponsor, you must demonstrate commitment to training Australian workers. You can meet this by:
Small businesses (<$10M turnover): Spend equivalent to 1% of annual payroll on training Australian employees
Large businesses: Spend equivalent to 2% of annual payroll on training
Pay the SAF levy when you nominate a worker (discussed in nomination stage)
Once approved as a sponsor, you must:

items.x: **Pay Market Salary Rate:** At least $70,000 or the Annual Market Salary Rate (AMSR), whichever is higher
**Provide Equal Terms:** Same terms and conditions as equivalent Australian workers
**Maintain Records:** Keep payroll, employment records for 2+ years
**Notify Changes:** Tell the Department within 28 days if sponsored worker stops working
**Allow Monitoring:** Cooperate with inspectors if visited
**No Cost Recovery:** Cannot require worker to pay visa costs, airfares, or other migration expenses
Business not lawfully operating or financially viable
Adverse immigration or workplace compliance history
Unable to demonstrate commitment to training
Insufficient evidence of business operations
Previous sponsorship breaches

blocks.x: Once your SBS is approved:

items.x: Approval is valid for 5 years
You can nominate multiple workers (no limit on numbers)
Each nomination requires separate approval
You can check your sponsorship status in ImmiAccount
Keep your ImmiAccount details secure

blocks.x: Your sponsorship can be cancelled or suspended if:

items.x: You breach sponsorship obligations
You provide false or misleading information
You fail to cooperate with monitoring
You have adverse workplace or immigration compliance issues

blocks.x: After obtaining SBS approval:

items.x: **Nominate a Position:** Lodge a nomination for the specific role and worker
**Worker Applies:** After nomination approval, the worker applies for their visa
**Maintain Compliance:** Meet all ongoing obligations throughout sponsorship period

seo.h1: Nomination Process for Employer Sponsored Visas

hero.h1: Nomination Process for Employer Sponsored Visas
intro: Comprehensive guide to the nomination stage of employer-sponsored visas including Labour Market Testing, SAF levy, occupation lists, and requirements.

blocks.x: The Nomination Process

Nomination is the second stage of the employer-sponsored visa process. After your business has Standard Business Sponsorship approval, you must nominate the specific position and the specific worker you want to employ.
A nomination is your formal request to employ a specific overseas worker in a specific position. Unlike sponsorship (which is about your business), nomination is about:

items.x: The **specific position** (occupation, duties, location)
The **specific person** (the worker you want to hire)
The **terms of employment** (salary, conditions, duration)

blocks.x: Each nomination is unique to one position and one worker. If you want to employ multiple people, you need separate nominations for each.

The old 482 short-term and medium-term streams are closed. Do not use the old short-term list or the medium and long-term list for a new 482. For a new Skills in Demand visa, the Core Skills stream uses the Core Skills Occupation List. The Specialist Skills stream uses ANZSCO major groups 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6. A 494 nomination uses the regional occupation rules for that visa.

For a nomination lodged from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, Core Skills pay must be at least AUD 79,423 and Specialist Skills pay must be at least AUD 146,576. A 494 nomination uses the Temporary Skilled Migration Income Threshold, which is AUD 79,423 in that period. The pay must also be at least the market rate for the job. These amounts do not include superannuation. See the [482 page](/employer-sponsored/sid-visa-482).
The salary must be:

items.x: Guaranteed base salary (excluding superannuation, bonuses, allowances)
For full-time work (38+ hours per week)
At least what you pay equivalent Australian workers
Commercially reasonable for the occupation and location

blocks.x: You must demonstrate:

items.x: The position is genuine and necessary for your business
You have a genuine need that cannot be filled by an Australian worker
The duties align with the nominated occupation
The role is not contrived to enable a visa

blocks.x: Labour Market Testing is required for:

items.x: Most 482 Core Skills and Specialist Skills nominations. Some are exempt. Do not use the old short-term or medium-term lists to decide this.
186 Direct Entry nominations
494 nominations

blocks.x: **Not required** for:

items.x: Some 482 nominations, where a trade agreement or another Home Affairs exemption applies. Check the [labour market testing page](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/employing-and-sponsoring-someone/sponsoring-workers/nominating-a-position/labour-market-testing).
186 TRT stream (transition from 482)
Positions under Labour Agreements or international trade obligations
Internal transfers (in some cases)
**Advertise the position** in Australia for at least 4 weeks
**Use at least 2 methods:** National recruitment website (e.g., Seek, Indeed) Local newspaper Industry-specific platform Professional association
**Timing:** Advertising must be completed no more than 4 months before lodging nomination
**Content:** Must include location, duties, salary (or salary range), and skills required
**Keep records:** Save all job ads, applications received, reasons for not hiring Australians

blocks.x: You must be able to demonstrate why Australian applicants were not suitable:

items.x: Didn't have required skills or qualifications
Didn't have required work experience
Didn't respond to interview invitations
Rejected job offer
Were not available to start when needed

blocks.x: The SAF levy is a mandatory payment that funds training for Australian workers.

items.x: Paid at time of nomination lodgement
Non-refundable even if nomination is refused
Calculated based on visa length requested
Regional 494: Higher levy ($3,000-$5,000 per year)
**186 Direct Entry:** $5,000 (small) or $10,000 (large) - one-time payment
**186 TRT:** No SAF levy required

blocks.x: In addition to SAF levy, there is a nomination fee of **$540** for all nominations.
Typical documents for nomination include:

items.x: Organizational structure chart showing where position fits
Detailed position description (duties, requirements)
Evidence of salary (employment contract or offer letter)
Labour Market Testing evidence (if required)
Evidence position is genuine (business plans, financial statements)
Market salary research (salary surveys, job ads)
Training evidence (for training benchmarks) OR SAF levy payment
**482 nominations:** 4-8 weeks
**186 nominations:** 4-8 weeks
**494 nominations:** 6-10 weeks
**407 nominations:** 3-6 weeks

blocks.x: Once your nomination is approved:

items.x: The worker can lodge their visa application (Stage 3)
You must continue to meet obligations (pay salary, maintain position)
If circumstances change (worker withdraws, business closes), notify the Department
The nomination is specific to that worker - you can't substitute someone else
Occupation not on relevant skilled list
Salary below market rate or $70,000 minimum
Insufficient evidence position is genuine
Inadequate Labour Market Testing
Position duties don't align with nominated occupation
Business not financially viable to support the position
SAF levy not paid or incorrect amount

hero.h1: Family and Partner Visas in Australia
intro: Bringing your partner, parents or children to Australia is personal, and the rules are strict. Our registered migration agents explain the visa options, the real costs, how long you may wait and what you promise as a sponsor, before you spend any money.

blocks.x: You may need a family visa if you are:

items.x: an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen who wants your husband, wife or de facto partner to live with you in Australia
engaged and planning to marry in Australia
an adult child who wants your parents to live in Australia
a parent or carer with a child overseas who needs a visa
an applicant with a relative in Australia who may qualify under a relative or carer category

blocks.x: Start with who you want to bring to Australia, then pick the group below. If you are not sure where you fit, [book a consultation](/book-an-appointment). A registered agent will tell you which options exist, and which do not.

Australian partner visas let the spouse or de facto partner of an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen live in Australia. You apply for the temporary visa and the permanent visa together, and you pay the visa application charge once. The Department usually assesses the permanent visa about 2 years after you apply, so it can check that the relationship is still genuine and continuing. Where the applicant is when you lodge decides whether you use the offshore visas (subclass 309 and 100) or the onshore visas (subclass 820 and 801).

sections.name: What sponsors must know
sections.h2: Being a sponsor: what you are agreeing to

blocks.x: The sponsor is the Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen who supports the application. Sponsors often do not realise what this means until the form is in front of them.

items.x: **You must be approved.** Home Affairs assesses you as well as the applicant, including police checks. Some criminal history, such as family violence offences, can stop a sponsorship.
**There are limits.** A sponsor can usually sponsor only a limited number of partners in a lifetime, and there is normally a gap of five years between sponsorships.

**You give a financial undertaking.** For partner visas the sponsor agrees to support the applicant for a set period. For parent visas an Assurance of Support (a bond and a financial promise) is usually required.
**You cannot just withdraw.** If the relationship ends, the visa process continues in some circumstances. Family violence provisions protect applicants in unsafe relationships.

sections.name: Proving your relationship
sections.h2: The four areas of relationship evidence

blocks.x: Case officers look at four areas to decide if your relationship is genuine and continuing:

items.x: **Financial.** Joint bank accounts, shared bills, shared loans or leases, how you support each other.
**Household.** Where you live, who does what at home, joint address on mail and records.
**Social.** Photos, invitations, travel together, statements from friends and family about your relationship.
**Commitment.** How you speak about the future, how you keep in contact when apart, your plans together.

blocks.x: No single document proves a relationship. We help you present a complete, honest picture, including when your situation is not typical (long distance, cultural marriage, separate addresses for work).

**Government charges.** Home Affairs sets these and changes them, usually each 1 July. A partner visa is one of the most expensive visas to lodge. Check the Department of Home Affairs website for the current charge.

**Other costs.** Budget for health examinations, police certificates, document translations and, for parent visas, private health insurance and the Assurance of Support. Our professional fees are separate and set out in a written agreement.
**Waiting times.** A partner visa decision commonly takes more than a year. Parent visas vary from a few months (870) to many years (103 and 804).
For the two-instalment parent visas, see our [cost for contributory visas page](/family-visa/cost-for-contributory-visas).

faqs.q: How long does a partner visa take?
faqs.a: It depends on whether you apply onshore or offshore and on how complete your evidence is. Many couples wait more than a year for the first stage, then the permanent stage follows about two years after you lodged.

faqs.q: How much does a partner visa cost?
faqs.a: The Department charges a single application fee for both stages, with extra charges for additional applicants. Health checks, police certificates and translations add to the total.

faqs.q: Can I live in Australia while my partner visa is processed?
faqs.a: If you apply onshore on a substantive visa you can usually stay on a bridging visa. If you apply offshore you usually wait overseas.

faqs.q: Which parent visa is fastest?
faqs.a: The Sponsored Parent Temporary visa (870) has the shortest wait but gives no permanent residence. Permanent parent visas take much longer.

faqs.q: Do I need to be an Australian citizen to sponsor?
faqs.a: No. Permanent residents and eligible New Zealand citizens can sponsor, as long as they are approved sponsors.

faqs.q: What happens if my relationship ends?
faqs.a: This depends on the stage and the reason. Special rules apply if there is family violence. Speak to an agent as soon as possible.

faqs.q: Do you guarantee a visa?
faqs.a: No. Only the Department of Home Affairs decides. We help you prepare the strongest honest application.

faqs.q: Can I switch from a visitor visa to a partner visa?
faqs.a: Often yes, but it depends on the conditions on your current visa. We check this at your consultation.

**Temporary visa.** The subclass 309 visa lasts until the Department decides your permanent subclass 100 visa.

Applications are processed in an order set by the Minister. See [family visa processing priorities](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-processing-times/visa-processing-priorities/family-visa).

The permanent visa is usually assessed about 2 years after you lodge the combined application. Those 2 years are a waiting period in the visa rules. They are not the same as the time taken to grant the temporary visa.

faqs.q: What is the Partner (Provisional) Visa Subclass 309?
faqs.a: It is a temporary visa. It lets the partner of an Australian citizen, permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen live in Australia while the permanent visa is processed.

faqs.q: Can I work or study on a 309 visa?
faqs.a: Yes, you can work and study in Australia without restrictions.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get the 309 visa?
faqs.a: There is no set time. Check the Department of Home Affairs visa processing time guide. Many partner visa applications take more than a year. The permanent visa is usually assessed about 2 years after you apply.

faqs.q: Do I need to be outside Australia when applying?
faqs.a: Yes, both application and grant must occur outside Australia.

faqs.q: Can I include children in my 309 visa?
faqs.a: Yes, dependent children can be included in the same application.

faqs.q: What happens after my 309 visa is approved?
faqs.a: You can live in Australia on the subclass 309 visa. About 2 years after you applied, the Department assesses the permanent subclass 100 visa. You usually need to give updated evidence. It is not granted automatically.

hero.badge: Offshore partner visa, stage 2
intro: Grants permanent residence to the spouse or de facto partner of an Australian citizen, Australian permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen.

blocks.x: The Partner (Migrant) visa (subclass 100) grants permanent residence to the spouse or de facto partner of an Australian citizen, Australian permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen. It is usually the second stage of the combined Partner visa application, following the grant of the temporary Partner (Provisional) visa (subclass 309). Once granted, you can live, work, and study in Australia indefinitely and later apply for citizenship if eligible.

In most cases, continue to be in a genuine, continuing relationship with your sponsor (Australian citizen, PR, or eligible NZ citizen)
Have met any condition and disclosure requirements since the 309 grant (e.g., no changes that invalidate the relationship)
Meet health and character requirements (you may be asked for updated checks)
Provide updated evidence of your relationship across financial, household, social, and commitment aspects
No outstanding debts to the Australian Government; sign the Australian Values Statement

If you were already in a long-term partner relationship when you applied, the Department may grant the permanent visa sooner. This usually means 3 years together, or 2 years if you have a child together.

If your relationship has ended because of family violence, your sponsor has died, or you have a child of the relationship, special rules may still let you be considered for the permanent visa. Get advice quickly.
Live, work, and study in Australia indefinitely
Access Medicare and domestic study pathways
Sponsor eligible family members for Australian visas
Travel to and from Australia freely; apply for a Resident Return Visa (RRV) after 5 years to maintain travel rights
Pathway to Australian citizenship once residency criteria are met
Full access to employment opportunities without restrictions tied to your partner visa stage
Track eligibility date: around 2 years after lodging your combined 309/100 application.
Look out for the Department’s request for further information for the permanent stage.

Obtain new police checks (and medicals if requested) for you and any dependents.

Upload documents in ImmiAccount under your existing application reference.

Wait for the decision; maintain a genuine, ongoing relationship during assessment.
On grant, receive your subclass 100 permanent resident status confirmed.

blocks.x: Pathway to Australian Citizenship

The subclass 100 visa is permanent residence. You can later apply for Australian citizenship if you qualify. Most people need 4 years of lawful residence in Australia, including at least 12 months as a permanent resident. Time spent outside Australia can affect this.
This is not a new visa application and it does not have a separate application queue.
The Department usually cannot grant the subclass 100 visa until about 2 years after you lodged the combined application.
It can be sooner if you were already in a long-term partner relationship when you applied. That usually means 3 years together, or 2 years if you have a child together.
The permanent visa is not granted automatically. You need to show the relationship is still genuine and continuing, unless a special rule applies. Get advice if the relationship has changed.

You do not lodge a new application for the subclass 100 visa, and you do not pay the partner visa base charge again. You paid that charge when you lodged the combined subclass 309 and 100 application.
You may still have to pay for police certificates, health examinations, translations and other documents if the Department asks for them.

blocks.x: The subclass 801 visa lets the spouse or de facto partner of an Australian citizen, Australian permanent resident or eligible New Zealand citizen live in Australia as a permanent resident. It is the second stage of the onshore partner visa. You apply for the subclass 820 and 801 visas together.

The Department usually assesses the subclass 801 visa about 2 years after you lodged that application. It is not automatically granted 2 years after the subclass 820 visa. You usually need to give updated evidence that the relationship is still genuine and continuing.

Once granted, you can live, work and study in Australia. You can enrol in Medicare. The visa does not expire, but the travel facility usually lasts 5 years from the date of grant. After that, you need a Resident Return visa if you want to leave Australia and return as a permanent resident. You can apply for citizenship later if you meet the residence and other rules.

After you become a permanent resident, you can apply for Australian citizenship if you qualify. Most people need 4 years of lawful residence in Australia, including at least 12 months as a permanent resident. Time spent outside Australia can affect this.

It can be sooner if you were already in a long-term partner relationship when you applied. That usually means 3 years together, or 2 years if you have a child together.

You usually need to give updated relationship evidence. The visa is not granted automatically. Get advice if the relationship has ended, including where family violence, the death of your sponsor, or a child of the relationship may be relevant.

items.x: Live in Australia temporarily while the parent’s permanent Partner visa is under process.
Study and work in Australia.
Travel in and out of Australia freely while the visa is valid.
Later be added to the parent’s permanent Partner visa application to gain permanent residency.

blocks.x: **Eligibility**

items.x: Must be a dependent child of a parent who holds a temporary Partner visa.
Must be under 18, or over 18 and financially dependent on the parent.
Must meet health and character requirements.
The sponsoring parent must have lodged a valid permanent Partner visa application with the same sponsor for the child.

Gather all the supporting documents.
Lodge the application and complete health and character checks.
Wait for the decision; once granted, the child can live in Australia until the parent’s permanent Partner visa is finalized.
When the parent’s visa is approved, include the child in that application to gain permanent residence.

seo.title: New Zealand Citizen Family (461) Australia | Bansal Immigration
seo.description: Temporary visa for people who are not New Zealand citizens but are members of the family unit of a New Zealand citizen.

hero.badge: Registered migration agents, Melbourne and Adelaide
intro: Temporary visa for people who are not New Zealand citizens but are members of the family unit of a New Zealand citizen.

head: Fact
Detail
rows: No set time. Check the Department's guide
Pathway to Further Stay in Australia

blocks.x: The **New Zealand Citizen Family Relationship visa (subclass 461)** is a **temporary visa** designed for individuals who are **not New Zealand citizens** but are members of the family unit of a New Zealand citizen who holds or is eligible for a Special Category visa (subclass 444).

This visa allows you to live, work, and study in Australia for up to 5 years, as well as travel in and out of Australia freely during its validity period. You can also apply for further subclass 461 visas to extend your stay, provided you continue to meet the eligibility requirements.

The subclass 461 visa is a great option for families wishing to live together in Australia, offering flexibility and access to key opportunities such as employment, education, and community participation while maintaining ties to New Zealand citizens residing in Australia.

sections.name: Eligibility
sections.h2: Do You Have What It Takes?

items.x: You are not a New Zealand citizen at the time of application
You are a member of the family unit of a New Zealand citizen (e.g., spouse/partner, dependent child, or certain dependent relatives) who is, or will be, in Australia
You continue to be a member of the New Zealand citizen’s family unit for the visa period
Meet health and character requirements (police certificates, health exams)
Have no outstanding debts to the Australian Government; sign the Australian Values Statement
If applying in Australia, hold a substantive visa or meet onshore application requirements
Live, work and study in Australia for 5 years from the date of grant
Travel to and from Australia as many times as you wish while the visa is valid
Include eligible family members in your application (fees apply)
Renew/apply again for another 461 to continue staying, if you still meet criteria
Confirm you are not a New Zealand citizen and you’re a member of the NZ citizen’s family unit.
Create/Use ImmiAccount (or import your paper application if lodged after 23 July 2025 update).
Gather identity, relationship, and dependency evidence; prepare police and health checks.
Complete the 461 application for primary and any secondary applicants.
Pay the visa application charge. The base charge is AUD 1,330.
Undergo health examinations with panel physicians (if requested/required).
Obtain and upload police certificates for all relevant countries.
Upload relationship and dependency documents (marriage/de facto evidence, birth certificates, proof of custody/guardianship).
Respond promptly to any Department requests for more information or biometrics.
Receive visa decision; on grant, live/work/study in Australia for 5 years and maintain eligibility.
**Initial Duration.** Temporary

blocks.x: Pathway to Further Stay in Australia

At the end of 5 years, eligible holders can apply for another subclass 461 if they still meet all relationship and eligibility criteria. This visa is not a direct pathway to permanent residence or citizenship; separate PR pathways may be available based on individual circumstances.

There is no set processing time. Use the Department of Home Affairs [visa processing time guide](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-processing-times/global-visa-processing-times). It shows how long recent applications took. It is a guide only, not a promise for your application.

Gather all the supporting documents for your application.
Lodge application offshore and pay fees.
Receive queue date and wait until your place is released.
After receiving the grant, migrate, live, and work in Australia permanently.

Access Australia’s Medicare (public healthcare).
Sponsor eligible family members to join you in Australia.
Apply for Australian citizenship when eligible.

You and any family members who are applying for this visa must meet health requirements.
You must be sponsored by your relative or their partner.

items.x: Confirm that you and your sponsor meet all eligibility criteria.
Obtain a medical assessment confirming your relative’s need for care.
Prepare and submit your application from outside Australia with all required documents (identity, sponsorship, health, and care evidence).
Pay the visa fee and wait for the Department of Home Affairs to process your application.
Once granted, you can move permanently to Australia to care for your relative.

blocks.x: The Aged Dependent Relative Visa (Subclass 838) is a permanent residency visa designed for single, older individuals who rely on a relative in Australia for financial support. This visa allows you to live permanently in Australia, sponsor eligible relatives, and apply for Australian citizenship if you meet the eligibility criteria.
Benefits of the Aged Dependent Relative Visa (Subclass 838)
The Subclass 838 visa offers numerous benefits, including:

items.x: Live and work freely: Reside and work anywhere in Australia without restrictions.
Indefinite residency: Renew your 5-year visa multiple times with no limitations.
Family sponsorship: Sponsor eligible relatives to join you in Australia.

Citizenship for children: Children born to permanent residents are automatically Australian citizens.

blocks.x: Eligibility Requirements for the Aged Dependent Relative Visa (Subclass 838)
To qualify for this visa, you must meet the following criteria:

items.x: Location Requirement: You must be in Australia (but not in immigration clearance) when you apply for this visa and when the Department makes a decision.
Sponsorship: You must be sponsored by an eligible relative or their partner who is an Australian citizen, permanent resident, or eligible New Zealand citizen.
Age Requirement: You must meet the minimum age to qualify for the Australian age pension.

Financial Dependence: You must have been financially dependent on your Australian relative for basic needs (e.g., food, shelter, clothing) for at least 3 years before applying. Financial dependence may also be due to a disability that prevents you from working.
Marital Status: You must not have a partner or spouse.
Visa Conditions: Your current visa must not include a no further stay condition .
Assurance of Support: You must be able to obtain an assurance of support from your sponsor.
Health and Character Requirements: You and any accompanying family members must meet the health and character requirements set by the Department of Home Affairs.
Outstanding Debts: Any debts owed to the Australian Government by you or your family members must be paid or arrangements must be in place to repay them.
Previous Visa Issues: You may not be eligible if you have had a visa refused or canceled while in Australia.

blocks.x: An ETA or eVisitor covers stays of up to 3 months at a time. A visitor visa (600) can be granted for longer. A visitor visa is not extended. You usually apply for a new one.

sections.name: What decides a visitor visa
sections.h2: The test behind every visitor visa

blocks.x: The Department of Home Affairs must be satisfied that you intend to visit Australia temporarily and then leave. This is the genuine temporary stay test in clause 600.211 of Schedule 2 to the Migration Regulations. The decision maker looks at your whole situation. No single document guarantees a grant.

head: What they look at
Evidence that helps
rows: Employer letter with approved leave and return date, recent payslips and tax returns, business registration if self-employed, proof of study
Recent bank statements showing steady funds, an explanation for any large or recent deposits, evidence of assets
Close family who stay at home, a travel history that shows you followed visa conditions

sections.name: Conditions to know
sections.h2: Visa conditions that catch visitors out

items.x: **Condition 8101 (no work).** You cannot work in Australia on a standard visitor visa.
**Condition 8201 (study limit).** Study is limited to 3 months.
**Condition 8503 (no further stay).** You cannot apply for most other visas while you are in Australia. A waiver is only given in limited, compelling cases.
**Condition 8558 (stay limit).** You cannot stay more than 12 months in any 18-month period.

blocks.x: Breaking a condition can lead to cancellation and make later visa applications harder. Check your grant letter for the conditions on your visa.

sections.name: Why visitor visas get refused
sections.h2: Common reasons visitor visas are refused

items.x: Weak ties to home, such as no job, no leave approval or no close family there.
Savings that do not match the trip, or unexplained deposits.
A vague itinerary, or one that does not match the stated purpose.
A history of overstays, refusals or breaches that was not explained.
A sponsor or host who has not shown their own status or relationship.
Answers on the form that do not match your documents.

blocks.x: A refusal stays on your record and is asked about in later applications. If you were refused, read our [visa refusal page](/appeals/visa-refusal) before you reapply. Our registered migration agents review your evidence, tell you honestly if it is thin and prepare a cover submission that addresses the genuine temporary stay test. We cannot guarantee any visa outcome.

faqs.q: Which visa do I need to visit Australia?
faqs.a: It depends on your passport and purpose. Some passport holders can use an ETA (601) or eVisitor (651). Others apply for a visitor visa (600). Young people from eligible countries may use a working holiday or work and holiday visa.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ETA 601 and eVisitor 651?
faqs.a: Both are quick online authorities for short visits. The ETA is for eligible non-European passports and is applied for by app, with a service charge. The eVisitor is free and for eligible European passports.

faqs.q: How long can I stay on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: It depends on the visa granted. ETA and eVisitor allow up to 3 months per visit. A 600 is usually granted for 3, 6 or 12 months. Condition 8558 may also limit total time.

faqs.q: Can I work on a visitor visa?
faqs.a: No. Visitor visas carry condition 8101. Business visitors can attend meetings and conferences, but they cannot do productive work or sell services to the public.

faqs.q: Can my parents visit me in Melbourne?
faqs.a: Yes, usually on a visitor visa (600). If you are an Australian citizen or permanent resident, you may sponsor them under the Sponsored Family stream. Our Sponsored Family guide explains what you need.

faqs.q: Can I extend my visitor visa?
faqs.a: Not in the usual sense. You apply for a new visitor visa before your current one ends, and condition 8503 may stop you. See our onshore visitor visa extension page.

faqs.q: How long does a visitor visa take?
faqs.a: Processing times change often. Check the Department's current global processing times before you plan.

faqs.q: Why was my visitor visa refused?
faqs.a: The most common reason is that the Department was not satisfied you would leave Australia. Book a consultation so we can read your refusal letter and explain your options.

faqs.q: Does each family member need their own application?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Each traveller, including children, needs their own visa or authority. Check the Department of Home Affairs website for how to apply for children, or ask us.

cta.title: Not sure which visa fits your trip?
cta.text: Tell us your passport, plans and any past visa history. We will tell you the right visa and what evidence you need.

seo.description: The Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) can review certain Australian immigration, refugee protection, character-related visa, citizenship, nomination.

intro: The Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) can review certain Australian immigration, refugee protection, character-related visa, citizenship, nomination, and sponsorship decisions made by the Department of Home Affairs or the relevant Ministers. It helps people who disagree with a decision seek a merits review.

blocks.x: What the Tribunal can review

The ART can review some though not all decisions made by the Department of Home Affairs and the Ministers for Home Affairs and Immigration. These include refusals and cancellations across visas and citizenship, as well as employer-related decisions like nominations and sponsorships.
Migration visa refusals or cancellations

If your application for a migration visa was refused, or your visa was cancelled, you may be able to ask the Tribunal to reconsider the decision. This can apply to various visa subclasses and circumstances depending on eligibility and time limits.
Protection (refugee) visa refusals or cancellations

Applicants whose protection (refugee) visas are refused or cancelled can seek review. The Tribunal reassesses the merits of the case, considering country information and any new relevant evidence permitted by law.
Character-related visa decisions

Where a visa is refused or cancelled on character grounds (for example, under section 501 of the Migration Act), the ART may review the decision. Reviews assess whether the original decision was the correct and preferable one in light of the evidence.
Australian citizenship refusals or cancellations

If your citizenship application was refused, or your citizenship was cancelled, you may be eligible for Tribunal review. The ART examines the decision against relevant criteria, including good character and residency requirements.
Nomination refusals

Employers and applicants can seek review of decisions refusing the nomination of an occupation, activity, or position associated with employer-sponsored visas. The Tribunal considers whether the nominated role and employer meet the program’s requirements.
Sponsorship decisions
The ART can review decisions to bar a sponsor, refuse to approve a sponsorship, or cancel an existing approval. This provides sponsors an avenue to challenge findings and present supporting evidence.
Applying, managing your case, and daily listings

You can apply for a review online, manage your case through the ART portal, and check daily listings to see hearing schedules and outcomes. Strict application deadlines apply refer to your decision notice for the time limit.
Language help and website translation

The website offers a translation feature for people who speak languages other than English. Important notes about accuracy and limitations are provided before using this tool to ensure you understand critical information.
Acknowledgement of Country

The Administrative Review Tribunal acknowledges the Traditional Owners and Custodians of Country throughout Australia, recognizing their ongoing connection to land, waters, and communities, and paying respects to Elders past and present.

items.x: **Strict Timeframes.** Appeals have short lodgement deadlines. We prioritise urgent lodgements to protect your review rights.
**Evidence Strategy.** We craft a targeted evidence plan aligned to tribunal expectations and decision‑maker concerns.
**Case Preparation.** From submissions to hearing preparation and representation, we manage your case end‑to‑end.
**Outcome Pathways.** We advise on negotiated outcomes, remittals and alternative pathways where appropriate.
**Urgent Assistance.** For cancellations, detention or s116/s501 matters, we mobilise rapid support.

**Visa Refusal.** Visa refusal occurs when an application for an Australian visa is declined by the Department of Home Affairs or a review tribunal. If your visa application is refused, you may have options to seek a review or appeal depending on the type of visa and grounds for refusal.

**Visa Cancellation.** Visa cancellation occurs when the Australian Department of Home Affairs or a review tribunal decides to cancel an existing visa, which may require the visa holder to leave Australia. Cancellation can happen for various reasons including character concerns, breach of visa conditions, or other statutory grounds.

**Notice of intention to Consider Cancellation.** A Notice of Intention to Consider Cancellation (NOICC) is a formal notification from the Department of Home Affairs informing a visa holder that their visa may be cancelled. It provides the visa holder an opportunity to respond before a final cancellation decision is made.

**Visa Refusal.** Visa refusal occurs when an application for an Australian visa is declined by the Department of Home Affairs or a review tribunal. If your visa application is refused, you may have options to seek a review or appeal depending on the type of visa and grounds for refusal.

Cancellation can happen for various reasons including character concerns, breach of visa conditions, or other statutory grounds.

**Notice of intention to Consider Cancellation.** A Notice of Intention to Consider Cancellation (NOICC) is a formal notification from the Department of Home Affairs informing a visa holder that their visa may be cancelled. It provides the visa holder an opportunity to respond before a final cancellation decision is made.

**Waiver Request.** A No Further Stay waiver request allows visa holders in Australia to ask the Department of Home Affairs to waive the No Further Stay condition on their visa, enabling them to apply for another visa while still in Australia under certain exceptional circumstances.

**Applying for Work Rights.** To apply for work rights in Australia, you generally need to demonstrate a compelling need, such as financial hardship, or be on an eligible employer-sponsored visa. Applications are made through the Department of Home Affairs, typically via Form 1005 or as part of your visa application process.

**Applying for Study Rights.** To study in Australia, you generally need to apply for a Student visa (subclass 500), which requires acceptance into a CRICOS-registered course, obtaining a Confirmation of Enrolment (CoE), and meeting financial and English language requirements. Applications are submitted online via ImmiAccount. For those on other visas, study rights depend on specific visa conditions.

seo.description: Guidance from the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia on appealing migration decisions to the Federal Court. An appeal challenges legal errors.

intro: Guidance from the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia on appealing migration decisions to the Federal Court. An appeal challenges legal errors in the original judgment; it is not a re-hearing and generally involves no new evidence.

blocks.x: What is a migration appeal?

An appeal asks the Federal Court to set aside a decision because the original Judge made a legal error. Appeals are usually heard by a single Judge, unless referred to a Full Court (three Judges). The appeal focuses on whether the law was applied correctly, not on re-deciding visa outcomes.
What the appeal Judge does and does not do

items.x: Does not decide whether a visa should be granted or cancelled.
Does not consider new evidence (except in special circumstances).
Does not call new witnesses.
Does read the documents filed in the original case and relevant transcript.
Does hear legal arguments from both parties.

blocks.x: What you must prove to succeed
You must show a significant legal mistake in the original decision (for example, applying the wrong legal principle) that justifies overturning the outcome.
If the Minister appeals
If you won your review, the Minister may appeal. You will receive a notice of appeal and become the respondent.
Legal advice and representation
You are strongly encouraged to obtain legal advice before appealing. Court staff cannot provide legal advice. A lawyer can:

items.x: Assess whether you have appealable legal issues.
Explain options, procedures, and likely costs.
Help draft a technically correct notice of appeal.

blocks.x: If you do not have a lawyer, free or low‑cost legal assistance may be available through community legal organisations.
Costs and fees
Appeals can be expensive. You must pay:

items.x: A filing fee when lodging the notice of appeal.
A separate setting‑down fee. If you lose, you may be ordered to pay the Minister’s legal costs.

blocks.x: Drafting the notice of appeal
Success depends on showing how the law should have been interpreted. Drafting grounds is technical and difficult, so legal assistance is recommended.
Additional resources and support

items.x: Federal Court website has more information about appeals.
Interpreters and accessibility support are available.
If documents were destroyed in a natural disaster, you can request replacements at no cost using the Natural disaster replacement document request form.
